title: Latent Handoff Protocols for Hosted API — PRD draft
content:
Purpose:
This doc sketches a proposal for a 'latent handoff' protocol to improve how the Hosted API coordinates incremental streaming responses, tool-call handovers, and structured output framing while keeping SDK ergonomics simple for client developers. The main goal is a robust, resumable, and observable handshake that enables low-latency tool execution and graceful degradation when capacity or connectivity is constrained.

Context and motivation:
- We have many existing PRDs for streaming semantics, typed tool contracts, and incremental output. Those cover pieces; implementation and SDK ergonomics remain fragmented.
- Real customer workflows require: partial outputs being actionable (e.g., show a bullet list while a tool is invoked), attaching structured metadata to parts of a stream, and resuming after brief disconnects without re-running expensive tool calls.
- Current friction: SDKs expose low-level stream frames but clients must implement complex state machines to coordinate tool-call lifecycles and retries. That increases error-prone client logic and server-side support burden.

Goals (what success looks like):
1) Define a minimal wire-level handshake between client, Hosted API, and optional tool providers that supports: incremental text frames, structured frames, tool-call intents, tool-call handoff acknowledgements, and resumable session tokens.
2) Provide a single high-level SDK primitive that handles handoff lifecycle for callers (including timeouts, retries, and local replay) with sensible defaults.
3) Ensure observability and debugging signals: per-frame trace IDs, per-handoff latency breakdowns, and clear errors for incompatible client/server versions.
4) Make server fallbacks straightforward: if a dedicated tool is unavailable, the runtime can fall back to a safe policy (e.g., use a cheaper model variant or decline to call the tool) while signaling partial results to the client.

Non-goals:
- This doc does not specify kernel-level runtime implementations (serving-runtime optimizations are out of scope).
- It is not a finalized spec for client libraries in every language; we provide one canonical JS/TS SDK pattern and reference ergonomics for other languages.

Personas:
- Frontend engineer building an assistant UI that integrates streaming text and tool results (autocomplete, tool widgets).
- Backend engineer wiring a task runner that must call internal APIs when the model requests external data (calendar/email).
- Platform engineer defining rollouts that degrade gracefully when tool capacity drops.

User stories (examples):
- U1: As a frontend engineer, I want to show partial answer bullets while a background tool call runs, then append the tool result when available without re-rendering everything or duplicating text.
- U2: As a backend engineer, I want to safely replay only the model tokens after the tool call failed to avoid re-running the tool if the model is re-asked for the same tool invocation.
- U3: As an SRE, I want telemetry that tells me which handoff (client->runtime->tool) experienced the latency so I can tune capacity and alerts.

Design overview (high level):
- Session token: A short-lived, resumable session token is negotiated at request start. It is opaque to clients but used for resumption and idempotency keys for tool calls.
- Frame types: We define a small set of canonical frame types that can appear on the streaming channel: TEXT_PART, STRUCT_FRAME (JSON metadata payload), TOOL_INTENT (declares model wants a given tool with args), TOOL_ACK (tool accepted), TOOL_RESULT (tool output structured), HANDOFF_END (tool interaction finished), ERROR_FRAME.
- Handoff flow summary:
  1) Client opens streaming request -> server issues session token.
  2) Model emits TEXT_PART frames while generating. When it emits a TOOL_INTENT frame, the runtime pauses high-confidence continuation and begins tool orchestration.
  3) Runtime issues TOOL_ACK to signal tool invocation scheduled and returns an interim STRUCT_FRAME to the client marking the tool call placeholder.
  4) Tool provider returns TOOL_RESULT which the runtime attaches as TOOL_RESULT frames and resumes TEXT_PART streaming, or substitutes structured content in place of a placeholder.
  5) If connection is interrupted, client reconnects with session token to resume. The runtime replays only model-derived frames up to the last confirmed TOOL_ACK; tools will be reconciled using idempotency tokens attached to the session.

Wire-level contract (informal sketch):
- Streaming channel uses SSE/HTTP2/WS depending on client. Each frame is JSON with: frame_type, seq, session_token (on the first frame if new), trace_id, payload (opaque string or structured JSON).
- Important fields (all strings):
  - frame_type: TEXT_PART | STRUCT_FRAME | TOOL_INTENT | TOOL_ACK | TOOL_RESULT | HANDOFF_END | ERROR_FRAME
  - seq: monotonic per-session integer for ordering
  - session_token: present on first frame and used for reconnection; server issues token (short TTL, e.g., 5m)
  - idempotency_key: optional string attached to TOOL_INTENT to allow tool providers to dedupe calls across reconnects

SDK ergonomics (JS reference):
- Provide a single high-level primitive: createHandoffStream(rpcOptions) -> returns an AsyncIterable of "events" and a client API to respond to SDK-level events. The iterable yields typed events: {type: 'text', text}, {type: 'struct', value}, {type: 'tool_request', tool, args, ack()}, {type: 'error', code, message}.
- The SDK handles: session token exchange, automatic reconnect/resume with exponential backoff, attaching idempotency keys to tool intents, and exposing hooks for custom tool providers.
- Default behavior: timebox tool calls to a runtime-configured timeout (e.g., 10s), render placeholder text to the UI while waiting, optionally surface a spinner tied to the tool_request event.
- Advanced: allow clients to register a local tool provider that will be invoked by the SDK (useful for browser-side connectors), or let the runtime forward tool requests to server-side integrations. The SDK hides the distinction under the same event surface.

Resumption and idempotency semantics (detailed):
- Reconnect flow: client reconnects with session_token and last_seq. Server validates token and returns frames from last_seq+1. If a TOOL_INTENT was in-flight but had no TOOL_ACK persisted before disconnect, the runtime will re-emit TOOL_INTENT with the same idempotency_key; tool providers must dedupe.
- Strong guarantee: tool providers implementing idempotency semantics will never run the same side-effect twice for a given idempotency_key. This is a best-effort guarantee when providers persist keys; document includes migration guidance.
- Weak guarantee: if a TOOL_ACK was returned (tool accepted) but the tool provider did not persist idempotency, on reconnect the runtime may re-invoke; SDK will surface a specific conflict error frame so the client can reconcile.

Fallback and graceful degradation policies:
- If tool capacity or a region is unavailable, runtime can: 1) return a DECLINE TOOL_ACK with a reason, 2) return a TOOL_RESULT synthesized by a cheaper model variant, or 3) fallback to a canned response.
- Policy config: per-route/organization, admins can configure default fallback strategy and safety checks.

Telemetry and observability:
- Each frame includes trace_id and handoff_id to correlate model->runtime->tool traces.
- Recommend built-in dashboards: fraction of sessions with handoffs, average handoff latency, tool invocation success rate, resumption frequency, and percent of sessions using fallback strategies.
- Telemetry should record: frames emitted, seq numbers at disconnect, idempotency_key usage, and tool provider responses.

Security and privacy notes:
- SESSION_TOKENs must be short TTL and tied to the original API key to avoid token reuse across accounts.
- TOOL_INTENT payloads may contain PII; recommend runtime redaction policies and labeling STRUCT_FRAMEs to indicate sensitive data.

Rollout plan and compatibility:
- Phase 0 (alpha): JS reference SDK + server feature flag in staging; enable for internal teams.
- Phase 1 (beta): Add server-side support for idempotency keys and tool handshake; expose SDK feature flag to selected customers.
- Phase 2 (general availability): default SDK primitive enabled; add language bindings and migration guides.

Acceptance criteria (examples):
- SDK can resume a streaming session after a simulated disconnect and continue from last_seq without re-triggering persisted tool side-effects for idempotent providers.
- Runtime surfaces clear telemetry for handoff latencies and fallback events.
- Frontend example app demonstrates rendering partial text and later injecting tool_result without duplicated text.

Open questions and tradeoffs to resolve:
- TTL for session_token (security vs. reconnect window).
- Scope and responsibilities for idempotency persistence: runtime vs. tool provider.
- How granular should STRUCT_FRAME schemas be? (freeform JSON vs. enforced typed contracts).
- Interoperability with existing non-streaming endpoints (how to translate).

Next steps and short-term TODOs (owner):
- Maya: prototype createHandoffStream JS API (2 weeks).
- Arjun: prototype server token handshake and persist basic idempotency metadata (2 weeks).
- Sofia/Ravi: implement telemetry primitives and dashboard mockups (3 weeks).
- Schedule a cross-team sync with serving-runtime and solutions-engineering to validate runtime assumptions (ASAP).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally pragmatic: single canonical SDK primitive + small set of frame types. Feedback requested on the frame set, idempotency model, and default SDK behaviors for timeouts/fallbacks.
- If you have immediate compatibility concerns with existing clients or retrofitting non-streaming routes, annotate comments inline or add JIRA links.
